Dad's Care Plan, Schedules and Helpers, in One Place

A one-page inventory of the papers, schedules and phone numbers behind Dad's care, and the ones you've never been given.

Download PDF

The care plan is in a folder at Dad's house, the agency schedule is a photo on your sister's phone, and the nurse's number is on a sticky note.

This page doesn't ask you to read any of it closely. It asks where each thing is, how recent it is, and who has it.

What to collectWhere it isIts dateWho has it
The care plan, in writing
Any assessment or summary you were given when the care was set up
The agency's visit schedule: days, times and what each visit is for
The agency's name and number, and the person who keeps Dad's schedule
The nurse, or whoever looks after the care plan, and how to reach them
Dad's doctors and his pharmacy, with phone numbers
Emergency contacts
Family, friends and neighbors who help, with phone numbers
Any visit notes or log kept at the house
Other written instructions you were given, such as discharge papers

Scroll sideways to see every column, or print this page to fill it in.

What's missing, and who will ask for it

Anything above with an empty line, and anything you've only heard about and never held. Put a name next to each.

For example The only copy of the schedule is the photo on Karen's phone. David will ask the agency for a printed one.

How to use it

  • Write the date printed on each item. If it has no date, write “undated” and ask for a current copy.
  • Don't rewrite or summarize a document here. Just say where it is.
  • For a phone number, note whose phone or which piece of paper it lives on, so anyone in the family can find it.
  • Keep this page with the papers, and bring both to the next conversation about Dad's care.

What this page doesn't do

It doesn't explain what any plan, schedule or instruction means, and it doesn't tell you whether what's on paper is what happens. If you read something you don't understand, that's a question for the person who wrote it.

Ready for the next step?

You know where the plan, the schedule and the phone numbers are, and which pieces you've never been given. The care interview puts them to use: it goes through Dad's situation area by area and turns your answers into a Family Care Profile you can bring to any care conversation.

Where this comes from

The rows for Dad's doctors and for emergency contacts follow what the CDC says a care plan should list. Keeping contacts and care details in one place follows the National Institute on Aging's suggestion of a shared notebook. The rest come from the Family Care Roadmap's working list for this step.

  1. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Steps for Creating and Maintaining a Care Plan
  2. National Institute on Aging, Sharing Caregiving Responsibilities
